title: Renouncing worldly cares for stillness
english: The Reasons for Monastic Life by Evagrius the Monk, the causes of things according to the monk, and the presentation of this [life] according to stillness. In Jeremiah it is said, 'And you do not take to yourself a wife in this place; for thus says the Lord concerning the sons and daughters born in this place: In a sickly death they shall die' (Jeremiah 16:2). This word shows that according to the Apostle, 'the married man cares for the things of the world, how he might please the wife, and is divided; and the married woman cares for the things of the world, how she might please the husband' (1 Corinthians 7:32-34).

And it is clear that not only concerning the sons and daughters who will be in the marital life is it said in the prophet, 'In a sickly death they shall die,' but also concerning the sons and daughters being born in their heart, that is, fleshly logismoi and desires, as they shall die in the sickly, weak, and dissolute mindset of this world, and these shall not attain the heavenly and eternal life. 'But the unmarried,' he says, 'cares for the things of the Lord, how he might please the Lord,' and he will make those who are chosen and immortal fruits of the heavenly life.

Such is the monk, and thus the monk must be, abstaining from woman, not making a son or a daughter in the aforementioned place; but not only that, but to be an incorporeal soldier of Christ, unconcerned, being outside of every worldly notion and practice, just as the Apostle says: 'No one having been enrolled for service entangles himself in the affairs of life, so that he may please him who enrolled him' (2 Timothy 2:4). In these things let the monk be, especially he who having left behind all the matter of this world, flees toward the beautiful and good trophies of stillness. For the asceticism is beautiful and good to stillness, how truly beautiful and good it is! For the yoke is good, and the burden is light; the life is sweet, the practice is straight.
Now, my beloved, you wish, then, for the solitary life...

As if one were to take up trophies and flee toward the things of stillness? Leave there the cares of the world, and the beginnings and powers over these things; that is to say, you shall become incorporeal, impassive, and outside of every desire; so that, having become a stranger to the commotion of these things, you may be able to be still well. For if no one spares himself from these, he would not be able to accomplish this same way of life.

Hold to the food of the few and the easily-provided-for, not of many and distracting things. And if even for the sake of hospitality a calculation concerning expensive things arises, leave this there, do not add to it at all; for through this the adversary lurks in you, he lurks to turn you away from stillness. You have the Lord Jesus rebuking the soul striving for such things like Martha (Luke 10:41-42), and saying: 'Why are you anxious about many things and troubled? One thing is necessary,' to hear the divine Word, and after this, to be sharp in all that is found. Therefore he also immediately brings forth saying: 'Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her' (Luke 10:42).

You also have the example of the widow in Sarepta (1 Kings 17:10-16), in what way she honored the prophet. Even if you have only bread, even if water, you are able to perform the reward of hospitality in these things; and if you do not have these, but only receive the stranger with a good intention and give him a useful word, just so you are able to provide the reward of hospitality; for a good word has been said instead of a house.

IV. Such things you must consider regarding almsgiving. Now, lest you desire to have wealth for the distribution of the poor—for this too is a deception of the evil one, often approaching toward vainglory and plunging the mind into the cause of busyness. You have in the Gospel testified by the Lord Jesus the widow (Luke 21:1-4), whose choice and power surpassed that of the rich through only two small coins. 'For they indeed,' he says, 'from their abundance cast in...'
